For one positive and 99 negatives, without ties, HR@10 = 1{s⁺ > s⁻₍₁₀₎}. Thus softplus((s⁻₍₁₀₎−s⁺)/τ)/log 2 upper-bounds the miss indicator pointwise. This algebraic bound is not a population calibration guarantee: I found no theorem establishing consistency for this exact softplus boundary loss. [Yang–Koyejo](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v119/yang20f.html) characterize top-k calibration and prove several seemingly natural top-k hinge surrogates inconsistent; unrestricted cross-entropy is consistent, but model restrictions can invalidate that guarantee. Smoothing an order statistic does not automatically inherit another surrogate’s proof.

Related work limits novelty claims. [Top-K Pairwise Ranking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.06709) aggregates comparisons across top-ranked scores and establishes Fisher consistency for its own objective under stated surrogate conditions; this does not establish consistency of a single-boundary HR loss. [Weston–Yee–Weiss’s k-order statistic loss](https://research.google/pubs/learning-to-rank-recommendations-with-the-k-order-statistic-loss/) already uses ordered samples to target recommendation quality, although it orders sampled positives rather than selecting the tenth negative. [SoftmaxLoss@K](https://jiawei-chen.github.io/paper/KDD25-SLK.pdf) combines quantile-based positive weighting with softmax loss. Its theory supplies conditional DCG bounds and quantile-estimation results, not unconditional Fisher consistency for sampled HR@10; its gradient-stability evidence is empirical.

Direct differentiation identifies optimization risks: away from ties, only the positive and currently tenth-highest negative receive direct score gradients, with magnitude sigmoid((s⁻₍₁₀₎−s⁺)/τ)/τ. The loss is continuous but nonsmooth when boundary identities switch; small perturbations can redirect the entire negative gradient. Ties require evaluator-specific treatment and implementation-dependent gradient allocation. Small τ produces stronger gradients on misses and saturation on comfortable hits; harder negatives receive no direct gradient until reaching the boundary. These are structural concerns, not proof of optimization failure. Guarantees must also match the 99-negative sampling distribution, rather than full-catalog ranking.
